CodeCommit.sourceTitle: What is AWS CodeCommit? - AWS CodeCommit
CodeCommit.summary: AWS CodeCommit is a managed AWS service for privately storing and managing source code, documents, and binary files in Git repositories. It provides Git workflows and AWS tools without requiring you to manage repository servers.
CodeCommit.explanation: You create a repository with the AWS CLI or CodeCommit console. Git then clones it to your computer. You edit files locally, stage and commit the changes, and push them to CodeCommit. Git pull downloads changes made by other users so your local copy stays current.
CodeCommit.syntax:
git clone <repository-url>
git add <files>
git commit -m "<message>"
git push
git pull

example.title: Clone and push a repository
example.code:
git clone https://git-codecommit.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/v1/repos/my-repository
cd my-repository
echo "Hello" > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"
git push
example.explanation: This clones a CodeCommit repository, creates a file, commits it locally, and sends the commit to CodeCommit.

useCases.title: Collaborative software development
useCases.scenario: A development team needs private Git repositories with code review before merging changes.

useCases.title: Git repository migration
useCases.scenario: A team wants to move an existing repository into an AWS-managed Git service.

useCases.title: AWS-integrated version control
useCases.scenario: A project stores source code and binary assets alongside other AWS resources.

interview.question: What is AWS CodeCommit?
interview.answer: AWS CodeCommit is a managed AWS service for private Git repositories. It stores and manages source code, documents, and binary files in the cloud.
interview.followUp: How does it reduce operational work? AWS manages the repository infrastructure, so you do not provision hardware or install and update server software.

interview.question: How does a normal CodeCommit workflow work?
interview.answer: Use the AWS CLI or CodeCommit console to create a repository. Clone it with Git, change files locally, commit the changes, and push them to CodeCommit.
interview.followUp: How do you receive another user's changes? Run git pull to synchronize the local repository with the CodeCommit repository.

interview.question: What collaboration features does CodeCommit provide?
interview.answer: CodeCommit supports Git functions such as branches, commits, pushes, pulls, and pull requests. Pull requests let users review and comment on changes before merging them.
interview.followUp: When might another AWS service be a better choice? Use Amazon S3 for large files that change often or for audit trails, because Git can require more processing as such data grows.

keyPoints: CodeCommit is an AWS-hosted version control service for private repositories.
CodeCommit encrypts repository data while stored and while transferred.
Pull requests allow team members to review and comment on changes before merging.
AWS manages the service infrastructure, so you do not provision or maintain repository servers.
You can use standard Git commands, AWS CLI commands, or CodeCommit APIs.
Existing Git repositories can be moved to CodeCommit.
gotchas: Do not use CodeCommit as a database. Git repositories grow as changes are recorded, so database performance can decline over time.
Avoid using CodeCommit for rapidly generated audit trails. Frequent automated changes can reduce repository performance.
A large number of branches or tags can slow repository operations. Remove branches and tags that are no longer needed.

CodeDeploy.summary: AWS CodeDeploy automates application deployments to EC2, on-premises instances, Lambda function versions, and ECS services. It supports in-place and blue/green deployment strategies.
CodeDeploy.explanation: You store deployable content in Amazon S3 or a supported source repository. CodeDeploy uses an application, deployment group, revision, and AppSpec instructions to deliver that content. The target depends on the compute platform: instances, a Lambda function version, or an ECS task set. For instance deployments, the CodeDeploy agent retrieves and installs the revision.

example.title: Start a deployment
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
aws deploy create-deployment \
  --application-name MyApp \
  --deployment-group-name MyGroup \
  --s3-location bucket=deploy-bucket,key=releases/app.zip,bundleType=zip
example.explanation: This starts a deployment from a ZIP revision in Amazon S3 to a named deployment group.

useCases.title: Server deployments
useCases.scenario: Release a server application to one or many EC2 or on-premises instances.

useCases.title: Lambda releases
useCases.scenario: Publish a new version of a serverless Lambda function.

useCases.title: Container deployments
useCases.scenario: Move production traffic to a new ECS task set.

useCases.title: Safer releases
useCases.scenario: Update applications while limiting interruption and keeping rollback options.

interview.question: What is AWS CodeDeploy?
interview.answer: CodeDeploy is an AWS service that automates application releases. It can deploy content to EC2 or on-premises instances, update Lambda function versions, or deploy ECS applications as task sets.
interview.followUp: How does it reduce release risk? It can shift traffic gradually, monitor configured health rules, and stop or roll back a deployment when errors occur.

interview.question: What are a revision and a deployment group?
interview.answer: A revision is the deployable application content, normally packaged with an AppSpec file. A deployment group identifies the target instances or the serverless or container resources involved in a deployment.
interview.followUp: What does the AppSpec file do? It describes deployment actions, including files, scripts, and lifecycle hooks appropriate to the compute platform.

interview.question: How do in-place and blue/green deployments differ?
interview.answer: CodeDeploy supports in-place and blue/green deployment types. In-place updates existing instances, while blue/green prepares replacement resources and then moves traffic to them; Lambda and ECS use traffic shifting such as canary, linear, or all-at-once.
interview.followUp: Which platform supports in-place deployment? Only EC2/On-Premises supports it; Lambda and ECS use blue/green deployments.

keyPoints: CodeDeploy automates releases to EC2 instances, on-premises instances, Lambda function versions, and ECS services.
A revision can contain code, Lambda functions, web files, configuration files, executables, packages, scripts, or multimedia.
Server-based application content can come from Amazon S3, GitHub, or Bitbucket.
The three compute platforms are EC2/On-Premises, AWS Lambda, and Amazon ECS.
The deployment types are in-place and blue/green.
CodeDeploy records deployment status, configuration details, instance health, and revision placement.
gotchas: Do not install the CodeDeploy agent for Lambda or Amazon ECS deployments. It is needed for EC2 and on-premises deployments.
In-place deployments are available only for the EC2/On-Premises platform. Lambda and ECS use blue/green deployments.
An EC2/On-Premises blue/green deployment requires Amazon EC2 instances, not on-premises instances.

Cognito.summary: Amazon Cognito identity pools give applications temporary AWS credentials with limited permissions. They support authenticated users and unauthenticated guest users.
Cognito.explanation: An Amazon Cognito identity pool gives an application temporary AWS credentials with limited permissions. It can use either an unauthenticated identity for guests or an authenticated identity after the application supplies identity-provider login tokens.

parameters.name: identityPoolId
parameters.description: The identity pool identifier, such as a regional Cognito identity-pool ID.

parameters.name: logins
parameters.description: An optional map from identity-provider names to the provider's login tokens.

parameters.name: clientConfig
parameters.description: Optional client configuration, including the AWS Region.

Cognito.returns: Temporary AWS credentials for application users. The resolved credentials also expose the Cognito identity ID.

example.title: Get credentials from an identity pool
example.explanation: This provider obtains temporary AWS credentials through the identity pool. The resolved credentials also contain the Cognito identity ID.

useCases.title: Temporary AWS access
useCases.scenario: A mobile or web app needs users to access AWS services without embedding long-term AWS keys.

useCases.title: Guest access
useCases.scenario: An app offers limited features before a user signs in.

useCases.title: Federated user access
useCases.scenario: An app accepts sign-in from a user pool or external identity provider and then calls AWS services.

interview.question: What does an Amazon Cognito identity pool provide?
interview.answer: An identity pool supplies temporary, limited-permission AWS credentials to an application. It supports authenticated identities and unauthenticated identities for guests.
interview.followUp: What makes the credentials temporary? The identity is exchanged through AWS STS using web identity federation, which returns temporary credentials.

interview.question: How does a JavaScript application obtain Cognito credentials?
interview.answer: Use the AWS SDK's Cognito identity pool credential provider. In the JavaScript SDK v3, this is the fromCognitoIdentityPool function from @aws-sdk/credential-providers.
interview.followUp: Where should the provider be configured? Attach it to each AWS service client through that client's credentials property instead of setting global credentials.

interview.question: When can an application retrieve the Cognito identity ID?
interview.answer: An unauthenticated identity can be retrieved immediately. For an authenticated identity, first set the identity-provider login tokens in the credentials provider, then retrieve the identity ID.
interview.followUp: How can the JavaScript SDK expose the ID? Resolve the client's credentials and read the identityId property.

keyPoints: Identity pools support two identity types: authenticated users and guest users.
An unauthenticated identity is suitable when the app allows guest access or does not need identity verification.
An authenticated identity comes from a verified sign-in through a user pool or another supported identity provider.
AWS STS exchanges the Cognito identity for temporary AWS credentials.
Guest applications can obtain an identity ID without first setting login tokens.
In the JavaScript SDK v3, read identityId from the credentials resolved by the provider.
gotchas: Give unauthenticated identities only the permissions that guest users need.
An identity ID alone cannot authorize AWS API calls; exchange it for temporary credentials.
On Android, perform these network operations on a background thread.

Cold Start.sourceTitle: Understanding the Lambda execution environment lifecycle - AWS Lambda
Cold Start.summary: A Lambda cold start is the setup work needed before a function runs in a new execution environment. It adds startup latency and can happen when Lambda cannot reuse an existing environment.
Cold Start.explanation: A cold start happens when Lambda prepares an execution environment before running a function. Lambda downloads the code, starts the environment, and runs initialization code outside the handler. After the invocation, Lambda freezes the environment and may reuse it for another request. A reused environment produces a warm start instead.
Cold Start.returns: The page does not define a return value for a cold start itself.

example.title: Detect a cold start
example.explanation: Create the utility outside the handler. The first call in a reused execution environment returns true. Later calls return false.

useCases.title: Cold-start observability
useCases.scenario: Measure or log whether an invocation is the first one in its environment.

useCases.title: Provisioned concurrency planning
useCases.scenario: Keep startup latency predictable for user-facing or latency-sensitive functions.

useCases.title: Initialization optimization
useCases.scenario: Move expensive setup outside the handler so it can be reused when Lambda reuses an environment.

interview.question: What is a Lambda cold start?
interview.answer: A cold start is the setup phase before Lambda runs the handler. Lambda prepares an execution environment, downloads code, starts the runtime, and runs initialization code outside the handler. A warm start reuses an already prepared environment.
interview.followUp: How can startup latency be reduced? Use smaller packages, optimize static initialization, or use provisioned concurrency when predictable startup time is required.

interview.question: What happens after a Lambda invocation?
interview.answer: Lambda freezes an execution environment after an invocation. It can retain and reuse that environment for a later request, which usually completes faster because setup has already happened. Reuse is not guaranteed.
interview.followUp: What state can be reused? In-memory data may remain available as a temporary cache, but code should tolerate its absence because the environment can be replaced.

interview.question: How does provisioned concurrency reduce cold starts?
interview.answer: Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes a chosen number of execution environments. This reduces cold starts and provides more predictable startup times. It increases resource cost because environments are kept ready.
interview.followUp: When is it most useful? Use it for workloads that need consistently low startup latency rather than occasional, best-effort warm reuse.

keyPoints: A cold start includes code download, environment setup, and initialization outside the handler.
Lambda freezes the environment after an invocation and may reuse it later.
A reused environment usually handles later requests faster than a new one.
Cold starts are uncommon overall, but their duration depends on the function and environment.
Cold-start duration can range from less than 100 milliseconds to more than one second.
Provisioned concurrency is the recommended option when startup time must be predictable.
gotchas: Cold-start setup adds both latency and billed invocation time.
Provisioned concurrency can initialize environments before requests, so initialization can occur before the first handled invocation.

Comprehend.sourceTitle: What is Amazon Comprehend? - Amazon Comprehend
Comprehend.summary: Amazon Comprehend is an AWS natural language processing service. It extracts information such as entities, key phrases, language, sentiment, syntax, and PII from documents.
Comprehend.explanation: Amazon Comprehend analyzes document content with natural language processing. It can detect entities, key phrases, language, sentiment, syntax, and personally identifiable information. You can use ready-made models or train custom models for classification and entity recognition.

parameters.name: Text
parameters.description: Text to analyze for real-time operations; the documentation's example operation uses text input.

parameters.name: LanguageCode
parameters.description: Language code for the input text, such as en.

Comprehend.returns: Analysis results such as sentiment, entities, key phrases, language, syntax, or PII, depending on the operation.

example.title: Detect sentiment in text
example.code:
import boto3

client = boto3.client("comprehend")
response = client.detect_sentiment(
    Text="The product works well.",
    LanguageCode="en"
)
print(response["Sentiment"])
example.explanation: This sends English text to Amazon Comprehend and prints the detected sentiment.

useCases.title: Find document topics
useCases.scenario: Group a document collection by recurring subjects.

useCases.title: Analyze customer sentiment
useCases.scenario: Measure whether customer comments are positive, negative, neutral, or mixed.

useCases.title: Study customer discussions
useCases.scenario: Find people, places, and products linked to topics in customer discussions.

useCases.title: Classify documents
useCases.scenario: Sort business documents using categories created for a specific application.

interview.question: What is Amazon Comprehend?
interview.answer: Amazon Comprehend is an AWS service that uses natural language processing to extract information from documents. It can identify items such as entities, key phrases, language, sentiment, and syntax.
interview.followUp: How can a team process a large document repository? Use an asynchronous analysis job rather than individual real-time requests.

interview.question: What is the difference between pre-trained and custom models?
interview.answer: Pre-trained models analyze common document insights without customer training data. Custom classification and custom entity recognition use existing customer data to build models for specific categories or terms.
interview.followUp: What manages repeated custom-model training? A flywheel orchestrates training and evaluation of new custom model versions.

interview.question: How can applications call Amazon Comprehend?
interview.answer: Real-time APIs suit small workloads, while asynchronous jobs suit large document sets. The Boto3 client exposes operations such as detect_sentiment and batch_detect_sentiment.
interview.followUp: What other AWS services can support a solution? The documentation names Amazon S3, AWS KMS, and AWS Lambda as integrations.

keyPoints: The service extracts entities, key phrases, language, sentiment, and other document features.
Supported insights include PII, targeted sentiment, and syntax in addition to common text analysis.
Custom classification lets you sort documents into categories defined by your application.
Custom entity recognition finds domain-specific terms and noun phrases.
Topic modeling groups documents into similar topics using word frequency.
Applications can use either the AWS console or the service APIs.
The service is designed for analysis at large document volumes.
gotchas: Text input must use UTF-8. Custom classification and custom entity recognition can also accept image, PDF, and Word files.
Choose real-time calls for small inputs and asynchronous jobs for large document collections.
Review the service's data-use terms before sending sensitive content.

Config.sourceTitle: How AWS Config Works - AWS Config
Config.summary: AWS Config records the state and relationships of supported AWS resources over time. It stores configuration data in Amazon S3 and sends selected notifications through Amazon SNS.
Config.explanation: AWS Config discovers supported resources and creates configuration items for them. It records later changes, including changes detected by periodic checks, and can evaluate resources with Config rules. It sends history and snapshots to Amazon S3 and notifications to Amazon SNS.

example.title: Inspect the AWS Config recorder
example.code:
aws configservice describe-configuration-recorders --region us-east-1
aws configservice describe-configuration-recorder-status --region us-east-1
example.explanation: Use these AWS CLI commands to inspect the recorder configuration and its current status in a Region.

useCases.title: Configuration history
useCases.scenario: Audit resource changes over time and inspect how related resources changed together.

useCases.title: Compliance evaluation
useCases.scenario: Check resources against required settings and identify noncompliant resources.

useCases.title: Change notifications
useCases.scenario: Process configuration-change events in an application or workflow.

useCases.title: Configuration snapshots
useCases.scenario: Create account-wide views of the current recorded resource state.

interview.question: How does AWS Config discover and track resources?
interview.answer: AWS Config first finds supported resources in the account and creates configuration items. It then records later configuration changes and keeps their history from the time recording starts.
interview.followUp: How can it notice changes that were not made through an API? It periodically checks resource configurations and creates items when it finds a changed configuration.

interview.question: How does AWS Config deliver recorded information?
interview.answer: AWS Config writes configuration history files and snapshots as JSON to a chosen S3 bucket. It also sends event notifications, such as configuration-item changes and compliance changes, through a chosen SNS topic.
interview.followUp: What happens when a change notification is too large for SNS? AWS Config sends a summary and stores the complete notification in the specified S3 location.

interview.question: How do AWS Config rules work?
interview.answer: A Config rule evaluates resource settings against desired conditions. Depending on the rule, evaluation happens after configuration changes or on a schedule, and the rule returns a compliance status.
interview.followUp: What happens when compliance changes? AWS Config publishes a compliance-change notification to the configured SNS topic.

keyPoints: When recording starts, AWS Config discovers supported resources and creates an initial configuration item for each one.
The default recording scope includes every supported resource in the Region, but you can choose specific resource types instead.
AWS Config uses resource Describe or List API calls to collect current configuration details.
A change can create items for the changed resource and related resources whose configurations are affected.
For each recorded resource type, S3 history is delivered in files covering six-hour periods.
SNS can deliver configuration-item change notifications within minutes, forming the configuration stream.
gotchas: Configuration changes are normally recorded soon after detection, but delivery is best effort and may sometimes take longer.
S3 history files are not sent when no recorded resource changed during the period.
You must manage S3 retention or archiving yourself with bucket lifecycle policies.

Control Tower.summary: AWS Control Tower APIs let you manage controls, landing zones, baselines, and tags with code. Controls target organizational units by ARN, and baselines can register OUs with Control Tower.
Control Tower.explanation: AWS Control Tower provides APIs and CLI commands for managing controls, landing zones, baselines, and tags. Controls can be applied to organizational units, while baselines can register and configure an OU programmatically.

parameters.name: controlIdentifier
parameters.description: ARN of the control to manage. The identifier is specific to a Region.

parameters.name: targetIdentifier
parameters.description: ARN of the organizational unit targeted by the control or baseline.

Control Tower.returns: API responses report the requested resource or operation status. Enabled-control responses preserve the identifier type used in the request.

example.title: List enabled controls
example.code: aws controltower list-enabled-controls --target-identifier arn:aws:organizations::123456789012:ou/o-example/ou-abcd1234
example.explanation: This lists the controls enabled for the specified organizational unit.

useCases.title: Manage controls
useCases.scenario: Apply governance rules to an organizational unit.

useCases.title: Manage landing zones
useCases.scenario: Create or update a landing zone through automation.

useCases.title: Apply baselines
useCases.scenario: Register an organizational unit with Control Tower.

useCases.title: Manage tags
useCases.scenario: Inspect or change resource tags.

interview.question: What can Control Tower control APIs do?
interview.answer: Controls are predefined policies that Control Tower applies to organizational units. The APIs can enable, disable, inspect, reset, and update controls.
interview.followUp: How do you identify the target? Use the OU ARN as the target identifier, together with the control ARN.

interview.question: What is a targetIdentifier?
interview.answer: A target identifier is the ARN of the organizational unit where a control is applied. The request must use the OU ARN for the target OU.
interview.followUp: What other identifier is needed? The control identifier, which is regional for each control.

interview.question: What are baseline APIs used for?
interview.answer: Baselines provide API operations for applying the AWSControlTowerBaseline baseline to an OU. This registers the OU with Control Tower programmatically.
interview.followUp: Are all baselines changeable? No. The baselines enabled for the landing zone during setup are read-only through these baseline APIs.

keyPoints: Control Tower exposes APIs for managing controls, landing zones, baselines, and tags.
Control APIs apply predefined controls to organizational units.
A control request needs the identifier of the control or guardrail.
The targetIdentifier is the ARN of the target organizational unit.
Landing zone APIs can configure and launch a landing zone.
The AWSControlTowerBaseline baseline can register an OU with Control Tower.
gotchas: Mandatory controls are fixed. You cannot add or remove them.
Control Tower returns the same identifier format that you used in the request.

Cost Explorer.sourceTitle: Analyzing your costs and usage with AWS Cost Explorer
Cost Explorer.summary: AWS Cost Explorer shows and analyzes AWS costs and usage. It supports graphs, reports, comparisons, CSV downloads, forecasts, and programmatic access through its API.
Cost Explorer.explanation: Cost Explorer reads AWS cost and usage data and shows it in graphs, tables, and reports. You can filter and compare the data, inspect trends, download CSV data, and forecast future spending. The console is free, but paginated API requests cost $0.01 each.
Cost Explorer.syntax: Cost Explorer console: AWS Billing and Cost Management > Cost Explorer

example.title: Request monthly cost data
example.code: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 --granularity MONTHLY --metrics UnblendedCost
example.explanation: This command requests monthly unblended cost data for October 2026 through the Cost Explorer API.

useCases.title: Analyze costs
useCases.scenario: Review spending by time period, service, or other available dimensions.

useCases.title: Forecast spending
useCases.scenario: Estimate upcoming AWS spending from past usage.

useCases.title: Find cost drivers
useCases.scenario: Investigate cost trends and unusual changes.

useCases.title: Use the API
useCases.scenario: Build scripts that retrieve cost and usage data.

interview.question: How do you enable Cost Explorer?
interview.answer: Open Cost Explorer in the AWS Cost Management console for the first time and choose Launch Cost Explorer. The console then prepares current and historical cost data. Cost Explorer cannot be enabled through the API.
interview.followUp: What additional feature is configured during enablement? AWS also configures Cost Anomaly Detection with an AWS services monitor and a daily summary alert subscription.

interview.question: What data and forecasts can Cost Explorer show?
interview.answer: Cost Explorer can display up to 13 months of historical data, the current month, and forecasted costs for future months. Forecasts are based on past usage and are estimates, not guaranteed charges.
interview.followUp: What can prevent a forecast? AWS may omit it when there is not enough data to support its 80% prediction interval.

interview.question: How can applications access Cost Explorer data?
interview.answer: The console lets you view and analyze costs through graphs, reports, filters, comparisons, and CSV downloads. The Cost Explorer API provides programmatic access, but each paginated request has a charge.
interview.followUp: How should an API client control cost? Identify the exact dataset before sending queries and avoid unnecessary pagination.

keyPoints: Use Cost Explorer to examine AWS costs and usage.
The console provides three cost and usage graph views.
Historical views can cover up to the previous 13 months.
Cost Explorer can forecast spending for up to 18 future months.
Download cost and usage data as a CSV file for detailed review.
Its data comes from the same dataset used for AWS Cost and Usage Reports.
gotchas: Every paginated Cost Explorer API request costs $0.01, so request only the data you need.
Recent billing data may be delayed because updates depend on upstream billing applications.
Enabling Cost Explorer cannot be undone.
A forecast may be unavailable when the account has too little historical data.

Direct Connect.sourceTitle: Dedicated Direct Connect connections - AWS Direct Connect
Direct Connect.summary: A dedicated Direct Connect connection links your network to AWS through a Direct Connect location. You choose its location and port speed, then use a virtual interface to access AWS resources.
Direct Connect.explanation: A dedicated connection links your network to AWS through a Direct Connect location. You choose the location and port speed when creating it, then use the issued LOA-CFA to arrange the cross-connect and create a virtual interface for AWS access.

example.title: Create a connection request
example.code: aws directconnect create-connection --location <location> --bandwidth 1Gbps --connection-name <name>
example.explanation: Creates a dedicated Direct Connect connection request at the chosen location and port speed.

useCases.title: Private VPC access
useCases.scenario: Connect an on-premises network to AWS private resources.

useCases.title: Public AWS service access
useCases.scenario: Reach public AWS services over a dedicated network path.

useCases.title: LAG-based connectivity
useCases.scenario: Combine several connections into one logical connection.

related: Letter of Authorization and Connecting Facility Assignment (LOA-CFA)

interview.question: What is an AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection?
interview.answer: A dedicated connection is a physical network connection from your network to AWS through a Direct Connect location. It lets you create virtual interfaces for public AWS services or VPC access.
interview.followUp: How can one connection reach multiple VPCs? Create a private virtual interface connected to a Direct Connect gateway, which can reach multiple virtual private gateways across accounts and Regions, except AWS China Regions.

interview.question: What must be selected when creating a dedicated connection?
interview.answer: You need a Direct Connect location and a port speed. Supported dedicated-connection speeds are 1, 10, 100, and 400 Gbps, and the selected speed cannot be changed after the request.
interview.followUp: What should you do if the required speed changes? Create and configure a new connection with the required port speed.

interview.question: What is the LOA-CFA used for?
interview.answer: After AWS processes the request, download the digitally signed LOA-CFA. Give it to the network or colocation provider so they can order the required cross-connect.
interview.followUp: When does billing begin? It starts when the port is active or 90 days after the LOA-CFA is issued, whichever occurs first.

keyPoints: A dedicated connection can use 1, 10, 100, or 400 Gbps.
Create the connection by itself or associate it with a LAG.
After the connection exists, create a virtual interface to reach AWS resources.
A Direct Connect location provides access to its associated AWS Region.
One connection in a public Region or AWS GovCloud (US) can access public AWS services in other public Regions.
A LAG lets multiple dedicated connections be treated as one logical connection.
gotchas: Choose the port speed carefully. To use a different speed later, create and configure a new connection.
Billing starts when the port becomes active or 90 days after AWS issues the LOA-CFA, whichever happens first.
If you have no equipment at the location, use an AWS Direct Connect Partner to establish the connection.

DocumentDB.sourceTitle: Amazon DocumentDB: how it works - Amazon DocumentDB
DocumentDB.summary: Amazon DocumentDB is a managed, MongoDB-compatible document database. A cluster uses a replicated storage volume, one primary instance for writes, and optional read replicas.
DocumentDB.explanation: Amazon DocumentDB separates database storage from compute. One cluster volume stores six copies of the data across three Availability Zones. A primary instance handles writes, while replica instances handle reads. The cluster endpoint follows the current primary after a failover, and replica set mode lets drivers use read preference and consistency settings.

interview.question: What are the main parts of an Amazon DocumentDB cluster?
interview.answer: A cluster has one virtual cluster volume and one primary instance. It can also have up to 15 replica instances. The volume provides storage, while instances provide database processing.
interview.followUp: How does the design support independent scaling? Add or remove instances to change compute and read capacity without resizing the cluster storage volume.

interview.question: Which endpoint should a normal application use?
interview.answer: Use the cluster endpoint in replica set mode with replica set name rs0. The cluster endpoint supports reads and writes and can redirect new connections to a new primary after failover.
interview.followUp: Why not use an instance endpoint? Its instance role can change after failover, so it is not suitable for production applications.

interview.question: How does DocumentDB store data and provide durability?
interview.answer: The cluster volume keeps six copies of data across three Availability Zones in one AWS Region. This replication supports durability and lets the cluster continue serving data if an Availability Zone has a problem.
interview.followUp: What happens when data is deleted? In DocumentDB 4.0 and later, allocated storage decreases by a comparable amount after data such as collections or indexes is removed.

keyPoints: A cluster contains one cluster volume and zero to 16 instances. Instances provide compute, while the volume manages stored data.
Each cluster has one virtual storage volume. It can store up to 256 TiB for engine version 8.0 and later, or 128 TiB for earlier versions.
The cluster volume spans multiple Availability Zones. Each Availability Zone contains a data copy.
The primary instance performs every data modification and supports both reads and writes.
A cluster can add as many as 15 read replicas. Replicas accept read operations only and can spread read workload.
The cluster endpoint points to the current primary and can move connection requests to a new primary after failover when an active replica exists.
Replica set mode makes the cluster appear as a replica set to clients. Its fixed replica set name is rs0.
gotchas: Do not use an instance endpoint for a production application. An instance can change from primary to replica after failover, so use the cluster endpoint in replica set mode instead.
The reader endpoint balances connections, not individual read operations. A connection may therefore send more work to one instance than another.
Replica reads can briefly be behind the primary. The documentation says lag is usually under 100 milliseconds, but high write activity can increase it.

example.title: Write, read, and query an item

import boto3
from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key

dynamodb = boto3.resource("dynamodb")

table.put_item(Item={"username":"janedoe","last_name":"Doe","age":25})
item = table.get_item(Key={"username":"janedoe","last_name":"Doe"})["Item"]
print(item)

response = table.query(
    KeyConditionExpression=Key("username").eq("janedoe")
)
print(response["Items"])

interview.question: How do you retrieve one DynamoDB item with Boto3?
interview.answer: Use get_item with the complete primary key to retrieve one item. In the example, the key contains both username and last_name because the table has a partition key and a sort key.
interview.followUp: How would you find several items for one partition key? Use query with KeyConditionExpression and a Key condition for that partition key.

interview.question: How do you change one attribute?
interview.answer: Use put_item to add or replace an item. Use update_item with an UpdateExpression when changing selected attributes, such as setting age to a new value.
interview.followUp: What is the difference between query and scan? Query selects items by key conditions, while scan examines table items and can apply a filter for attributes.

interview.question: How can Boto3 write many items efficiently?
interview.answer: Use batch_writer as a context manager. Call put_item or delete_item on the batch object; it buffers requests, sends them in batches, and retries unprocessed items.
interview.followUp: How do you filter a scan by a non-key attribute? Import Attr and pass a FilterExpression such as Attr('age').lt(27).

Use Key for conditions on keys and Attr for conditions on other attributes.
gotchas: A Table resource for an existing table does not request or populate table attributes until you access them or call load().
The batch writer retries unprocessed items, but it is intended for batch writes rather than conditional update logic.

interview.question: What are the EBS direct APIs used for?
interview.answer: The EBS direct APIs allow software to create snapshots, write data to snapshots, read snapshot data, and compare two snapshots. They avoid creating new volumes and EC2 instances just to find changes.
interview.followUp: Why are these APIs useful for backup software? They can track incremental volume changes through snapshots, which can reduce copying work and cost.

interview.question: Which AWS CLI commands are available under ebs?
interview.answer: The command set includes start-snapshot and complete-snapshot for snapshot creation. It also includes put-snapshot-block, get-snapshot-block, list-changed-blocks, and list-snapshot-blocks for block operations.
interview.followUp: How could a disaster-recovery workflow use them? It could write on-premises data to a snapshot during an outage and restore it after recovery.

interview.question: How can the APIs support incremental backups?
interview.answer: A parent snapshot can be supplied when starting a snapshot to create an incremental snapshot. The APIs can then identify differences between snapshots.
interview.followUp: What alternative do these APIs avoid? They avoid creating volumes from snapshots and using EC2 instances to compare those volumes.

keyPoints: The APIs support snapshot creation plus direct block reads and writes.
You can find which blocks changed between two snapshots.
Comparing snapshot changes does not require creating temporary EBS volumes.
The direct API approach does not need EC2 instances for snapshot comparison.
Backup software can create incremental snapshots from on-premises data.

interview.question: What is an Amazon ECS task definition?
interview.answer: A task definition is a JSON blueprint for an ECS application. It describes the containers, images, ports, operating system settings, and volumes used by the task.
interview.followUp: How does a service use a task definition? A service launches tasks from the definition and replaces stopped or failed tasks to maintain the desired count.

interview.question: What is an ECS cluster?

interview.question: What is the difference between a task and a service?

interview.question: What does Amazon EKS manage?
interview.answer: EKS standard leaves AWS responsible for the Kubernetes control plane. AWS handles control-plane components and keeps the cluster running, while you manage the worker compute and workloads.

interview.question: How does EKS handle access control?

interview.question: How does an EC2 application connect to an ElastiCache cache?
interview.answer: Use an EC2 instance in the cache's VPC and configure security-group inbound rules for the cache protocol's ports. Valkey and Redis OSS use port 6379 for node-based clusters; Memcached uses port 11211.
interview.followUp: What changes for ElastiCache Serverless? Allow port 6379 for the primary endpoint and port 6380 for the read-optimized endpoint.

interview.question: Which ports does ElastiCache use?
interview.answer: Use port 6379 for Valkey or Redis OSS commands. For serverless caches, port 6379 handles writes and strongly consistent reads, while port 6380 supports read-from-replica requests with eventual consistency.
interview.followUp: Why might port 6380 still be required? Many clients connect to both serverless ports even when read-from-replica is not enabled.

interview.question: Why must the command-line client support TLS?
interview.answer: The documentation recommends valkey-cli and says to compile it with TLS support. A serverless cache requires TLS, so the client must support encrypted connections.
interview.followUp: What if the cache is not encrypted? The TLS build option is not needed for a non-encrypted cluster.

keyPoints: ElastiCache manages and scales distributed in-memory cache environments.
The service provides an in-memory cache without requiring you to manage the cache infrastructure yourself.
Applications and tools that use Redis or Memcached protocols can work with the matching ElastiCache service.
Node-based Valkey and Redis OSS clusters accept commands on port 6379.
Memcached uses ports 11211 and 11212 for commands.
Serverless port 6380 is intended for lower-latency replica reads with eventual consistency.

Event Source Mapping.sourceTitle: How Lambda processes records from stream and queue-based event sources - AWS Lambda
Event Source Mapping.summary: Lambda event source mappings poll supported streams and queues, then invoke a function with batches of records. Lambda ends a batch when its time, record count, or 6 MB payload limit is reached.
Event Source Mapping.explanation: Lambda uses an event source mapping to poll a supported stream or queue, collect records, and invoke a function with a batch. It invokes the function when the batching window ends, the batch reaches its size, or the payload reaches 6 MB. Failed batches can be retried, so function code should safely handle duplicates.

parameters.name: --function-name
parameters.description: The Lambda function name or ARN that receives records.

parameters.name: --event-source-arn
parameters.description: The ARN of the stream, queue, broker, cluster, or change stream.

parameters.name: --batch-size
parameters.description: Maximum records in one batch; valid range is 1 to 10,000, with service-specific defaults and limits.

parameters.name: --maximum-batching-window-in-seconds
parameters.description: Maximum collection time in seconds, from 0 through 300.

parameters.name: --starting-position
parameters.description: Starting stream position: TRIM_HORIZON, LATEST, or AT_TIMESTAMP where supported.

parameters.name: --enabled / --no-enabled
parameters.description: Whether the mapping polls and invokes the function.

Event Source Mapping.returns: The mapping is created and Lambda reads records from the configured source to invoke the function. The mapping API exposes its identifier, state, batch settings, source, function, and processing result.

example.title: Create an SQS event source mapping
example.code:
aws lambda create-event-source-mapping \
  --function-name process-orders \
  --event-source-arn arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:123456789012:orders \
  --batch-size 10 \
  --maximum-batching-window-in-seconds 0
example.explanation: This command creates an enabled mapping that reads an SQS queue and sends up to 10 records per function call.

interview.question: What is an event source mapping?
interview.answer: An event source mapping is a Lambda resource that polls a supported stream or queue and invokes a function with record batches. It is managed by Lambda, unlike a direct trigger, where the source service pushes the event.
interview.followUp: Why use batches? Batching reduces per-invocation overhead and can improve throughput when the function can process several records together.

interview.question: When does Lambda invoke the function?
interview.answer: Lambda invokes the function when the batching window expires, the configured batch size is reached, or the payload reaches 6 MB. The window is the maximum collection time, while batch size is the maximum record count.
interview.followUp: What happens if records arrive slowly? Lambda waits only until the configured window expires, then invokes with the records collected so far.

interview.question: How should a function handle failures?
interview.answer: Lambda processes records at least once, so duplicate delivery is possible. For stream sources, a failed batch can be retried and the affected shard can pause to preserve order.
interview.followUp: How can partial progress be reported? Supported mappings can use ReportBatchItemFailures so the function identifies failed records instead of treating the whole batch as failed.

keyPoints: Mappings connect Lambda functions to streams and queues, then send records in batches.
An invocation starts when the time limit, record limit, or 6 MB payload limit is reached.
Kinesis, DynamoDB, and SQS invoke as soon as records are available by default.
MSK, self-managed Kafka, MQ, and DocumentDB use a 500 ms default window.
Lambda normally adjusts event pollers automatically as traffic changes.
Provisioned mode lets supported Kafka and SQS mappings set poller limits.
gotchas: Processing is at least once. A record may be delivered again, so make the function idempotent.
The payload limit is fixed at 6 MB. A batch can end before its record count or time limit.
An extension can still run when the next batch starts. This can raise concurrency and cause throttling.
For stream sources, a failed batch can pause its shard while Lambda retries the batch.

interview.question: What is AWS Fargate?
interview.answer: Fargate is an ECS technology for running containers without managing EC2 servers or clusters. You specify the container image, CPU, memory, networking, and IAM settings, then launch the task.
interview.followUp: What isolation does a Fargate task provide? Each task has its own isolation boundary and does not share the underlying kernel, CPU resources, memory resources, or elastic network interface with another task.

interview.question: How do you configure an ECS task for Fargate?
interview.answer: Set the task definition's requiresCompatibilities parameter to FARGATE. Fargate task definitions also use the awsvpc network mode, so each task receives an elastic network interface.
interview.followUp: How should a load balancer target these tasks? Use a target group with target type ip because the task is associated with an elastic network interface rather than an EC2 instance.

interview.question: What capacity providers are available for Fargate?
interview.answer: Fargate provides Fargate and Fargate Spot capacity providers. Fargate Spot uses spare compute capacity and can interrupt tasks with a two-minute warning when AWS needs that capacity back.
interview.followUp: Which workloads fit Fargate Spot? Use it for tasks that tolerate interruption, such as retryable or fault-tolerant batch work.

keyPoints: Fargate lets ECS run containers without requiring you to provision or manage servers.
Each task has a separate isolation boundary and does not share the host kernel, CPU, memory, or network interface with another task.
A task definition selects Fargate by setting requiresCompatibilities to FARGATE.

interview.answer: GetObjectCommand reads one object from an S3 bucket. Set Bucket to the bucket name and Key to the object name, then send the command with an S3Client.
interview.followUp: How can a request avoid downloading an unchanged object? Add IfMatch or IfNoneMatch with the object's ETag and handle the resulting service response.

interview.question: What is the Boto3 GlobalAccelerator client?
interview.answer: The client represents the low-level AWS Global Accelerator API. It provides operations for creating and managing accelerators, listeners, endpoint groups, endpoints, and custom-routing resources.
interview.followUp: What region should the client use? Use us-west-2, because Global Accelerator requires the US West (Oregon) Region for accelerator operations.

interview.question: How does a standard accelerator choose an endpoint?
interview.answer: A standard accelerator routes traffic to suitable regional endpoints through the AWS global network. It considers endpoint health, client location, and configured policies.
interview.followUp: What happens when endpoint health changes? Global Accelerator reacts to health or configuration changes and directs traffic to healthy endpoints.

interview.question: What static addresses does Global Accelerator provide?

interview.followUp: What happens to these addresses after deletion? They are lost when the accelerator is deleted, so they cannot be used to route traffic afterward.

A standard accelerator sends traffic through the AWS global network to suitable endpoints.
A custom routing accelerator lets application logic select a specific endpoint.
An IPv4 accelerator receives two static IPv4 addresses.
A dual-stack accelerator receives four addresses: two IPv4 and two IPv6.
Routing responds to endpoint health and configuration changes.

Deleting an accelerator permanently removes its assigned static IP addresses.

interview.question: What is Amazon GuardDuty?
interview.answer: GuardDuty is a threat detection service for AWS. It continuously analyzes supported logs and data sources, then creates findings when it identifies potentially suspicious or malicious activity.
interview.followUp: What happens to foundational data sources after enabling GuardDuty? GuardDuty begins ingesting supported CloudTrail management events, VPC flow logs, and DNS logs without separate setup.

interview.question: What does it mean that GuardDuty is Regional?

interview.question: What is a GuardDuty finding and how can you manage it?

IAM.summary: AWS IAM controls access to AWS resources with JSON policies. Requests are allowed only when applicable policies allow them and no applicable policy explicitly denies them.
IAM.explanation: IAM controls access to AWS resources with policies. A request is allowed only when applicable policies allow it and no policy explicitly denies it. Permissions boundaries, organization SCPs, and session policies can further limit an allow.

interview.question: How does IAM decide whether to allow a request?
interview.answer: IAM authenticates the principal and then checks authorization. Applicable identity and resource policies are evaluated, and an explicit deny wins over any allow.
interview.followUp: What can limit an allowed request? A permissions boundary, organization SCP, or session policy can impose an additional limit.

interview.question: What is an IAM policy?
interview.answer: Policies are JSON documents that define permissions. You attach them to IAM identities or AWS resources.
interview.followUp: What happens without an allow? The request remains implicitly denied unless the root-user default applies.

interview.question: What is needed for cross-account access?
interview.answer: A cross-account request requires permission from the resource-owning account. The identity used to make the request must also be allowed to make that request.
interview.followUp: Why can an allow still fail? An explicit deny or a limiting boundary, SCP, or session policy can override the allow.

IAM evaluates policy rules against the request context.
An applicable allow changes the default implicit denial.
Boundaries, SCPs, and session policies can restrict an otherwise allowed request.

A principal needs an applicable allow policy before it can use a resource.
Cross-account access needs permission in the target account and permission for the calling identity to make the request.

interview.followUp: How does it help with multiple accounts? Permission sets define common permissions, and administrators assign users or groups to accounts centrally.

interview.question: How does IAM Identity Center work with the AWS CLI?
interview.answer: A user signs in through the AWS access portal. IAM Identity Center maps the identity to assigned permission sets and provides temporary access for AWS tools or applications.
interview.followUp: What happens in the AWS CLI? The CLI uses the assumed role linked to the configured profile until the session expires.

interview.question: What is the difference between organization and account instances?
interview.answer: An organization instance is deployed from the AWS Organizations management account and supports account access management across AWS. An account instance belongs to one AWS account and is intended for isolated application deployments.
interview.followUp: Which instance should production use? The documentation recommends an organization instance for production application use and account access management.

Kinesis.summary: A Ruby AWS Lambda function can consume records from a Kinesis stream. It reads each record, decodes its Base64 payload, and processes the resulting data.
Kinesis.explanation: A Lambda function can receive a batch of records from a Kinesis stream. For each record, it reads the encoded payload, decodes it from Base64, and then processes the resulting data. If processing fails, the function can return the failed record's sequence number so Lambda retries from that record.

example.title: Read Kinesis records in Lambda
example.code:
def lambda_handler(event:, context:)
  event['Records'].each do |record|
    data = Base64.decode64(record['kinesis']['data']).force_encoding('UTF-8')
    puts data
  end
end
example.explanation: This Ruby Lambda handler reads each Kinesis record, decodes its Base64 data, and prints the result.

interview.question: How does a Ruby Lambda function read Kinesis data?
interview.answer: The handler loops through event['Records']. For each record, it reads record['kinesis']['data'] and decodes the Base64 value before processing it.
interview.followUp: What should the function return after a record fails? Return a batchItemFailures response containing the failed record's sequence number.

interview.question: How can a Lambda function report a failed Kinesis record?
interview.answer: The function can return the failed record's sequence number in batchItemFailures. Lambda uses that identifier to retry the failed item and later items in the stream batch.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful for streams? It preserves ordered retry behavior from the failed record instead of treating the whole batch as successfully processed.

interview.question: What structure does a Kinesis event use in the Ruby example?
interview.answer: The event contains a Records collection, so the handler processes records one at a time. The record payload is under the nested kinesis object and must be decoded from Base64.
interview.followUp: What additional behavior should production code add? It should handle processing errors and raise or return an appropriate failure response so the event is retried.

keyPoints: A Lambda function can be triggered when records arrive in a Kinesis stream.
The record payload must be Base64-decoded before the application uses it.
The handler processes every record in the event's Records collection.
A Kinesis record has a sequence number that identifies its position in the stream.

interview.question: What problem does AWS KMS solve?
interview.answer: AWS KMS creates, manages, uses, and deletes KMS keys within the service. Those keys do not leave KMS in unencrypted form, and KMS protects them with validated hardware security modules.
interview.followUp: How can applications call KMS? They can use the console, AWS CLI, REST API, or AWS SDKs, provided the caller has the required permissions.

interview.question: How can a program access AWS KMS?
interview.answer: The console is a web interface for managing KMS and AWS resources. API, CLI, and SDK users need permission to call the relevant KMS operations; they do not need the console's minimum permissions.
interview.followUp: What can happen immediately after a KMS resource change? Because the API is eventually consistent, a subsequent request can briefly fail until the change propagates.

interview.question: What is the AWS Encryption SDK's role?
interview.answer: The AWS Encryption SDK performs client-side encryption and integrates with KMS. It does not expose all KMS capabilities.
interview.followUp: What is the difference between the SDK and the REST API? SDK libraries wrap the REST API and simplify programmatic requests, while the REST API is the underlying HTTP interface.

keyPoints: AWS KMS manages keys used for encryption and signing.
KMS keys remain inside AWS KMS and are not exposed there in plaintext.
KMS protects created keys with FIPS 140-3 Security Level 3 validated HSMs.
The REST API lets clients use HTTP requests to work with KMS.

gotchas: KMS uses eventual consistency. A change may take seconds, and sometimes minutes, to become visible. A following request can temporarily return errors such as NotFoundException or InvalidStateException.
The AWS Encryption SDK is not a complete interface to KMS. It integrates with KMS for client-side encryption, but it can also operate without KMS keys.

interview.question: What does AWS Lake Formation control?
interview.answer: Lake Formation controls access to Data Catalog resources and can manage access to their Amazon S3 data. It replaces complex combinations of S3 bucket policies and IAM policies for managed data.
interview.followUp: What happens when a query runs? The engine gets metadata after a permission check, then receives temporary access for registered data and reads the permitted data from S3.

interview.question: How does permission checking work during a query?
interview.answer: The engine first asks the Data Catalog for metadata. The catalog checks Lake Formation permissions and returns only metadata the user may see.
interview.followUp: What happens after metadata authorization? For registered data, the engine requests temporary access and then reads from Amazon S3.

interview.question: What is credential vending?
interview.answer: Credential vending means Lake Formation gives an integrated analytical engine temporary access to registered Amazon S3 data. The engine uses that access to read data and apply row, column, or cell filtering.
interview.followUp: What is the alternative for an unmanaged table? The engine accesses S3 directly, and S3 and IAM policies decide whether access is allowed.

keyPoints: Lake Formation uses a database-style permission model for data lake resources.
Permissions can be granted or removed at the database, table, and column levels.
One control layer protects catalog metadata.
Another control layer manages access to the data stored in Amazon S3.
During a query, the Data Catalog checks the user's Lake Formation permissions.

The engine reads from S3 and applies the required data filtering.
gotchas: Tables not managed by Lake Formation use the Amazon S3 bucket policy and IAM policy path instead of Lake Formation credential vending.

interview.question: What is AWS Lambda?
interview.answer: AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service. It runs code without requiring the customer to provision or manage servers, while AWS handles infrastructure tasks such as capacity, scaling, maintenance, and patching.
interview.followUp: How does Lambda scale Event Functions? Lambda creates and removes execution environments as demand changes, scaling horizontally across independent invocations.

interview.question: How does a Lambda Event Function run?
interview.answer: An Event Function runs a handler when an event or API call invokes it. Common integrations include API Gateway, Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, and EventBridge.
interview.followUp: How does an Event Function differ from a Web Function? An Event Function uses a handler invocation model, while a Web Function is an HTTP server that listens on a port and serves concurrent requests.

interview.question: Can an Event Function keep state between invocations?
interview.answer: Lambda manages the lifecycle of Event Function execution environments. An environment can be reused for a warm start, but application state should not be assumed to survive between invocations.
interview.followUp: What should an application do with persistent state? Store required state in an external durable service instead of relying on an execution environment's memory or disk.

keyPoints: Lambda is a serverless compute service for running application code without managing servers.
AWS manages server maintenance, capacity provisioning, scaling, and patching for Lambda workloads.
Event Functions use a handler that Lambda invokes after an event or API request.
Invocations are independent and can scale horizontally to meet demand.

interview.question: Which interfaces can manage Lightsail resources?
interview.answer: Lightsail can be managed through the web console, AWS CLI, CloudShell, Query API, SDKs, and AWS Tools for PowerShell. The CLI works from Windows, Mac, and Linux shells.
interview.followUp: How would you run CLI commands without installing the CLI locally? Use AWS CloudShell, which is a browser-based shell launched from the AWS Management Console.

interview.question: What is the difference between Lightsail IPv4 and dual-stack endpoints?
interview.answer: Lightsail has regional IPv4 endpoints and dual-stack endpoints. IPv4 endpoints accept IPv4 traffic, while dual-stack endpoints accept IPv4 and IPv6 traffic.
interview.followUp: What happens if the endpoint is omitted? The IPv4 endpoint is selected by default.

interview.question: How are Lightsail service endpoints formed?
interview.answer: The regional IPv4 endpoint follows `lightsail.region.amazonaws.com`. The dual-stack endpoint follows `lightsail.region.api.aws`; for example, the US East (Ohio) endpoints use `lightsail.us-east-2.amazonaws.com` and `lightsail.us-east-2.api.aws`.

interview.question: How is Macie scoped?
interview.answer: Macie has one session per AWS account and Region. Enabling Macie starts its activities in that Region and creates the session.
interview.followUp: What happens when Macie is paused? Macie stops its activities but keeps the session identifier, settings, resources, and certain stored data.

interview.question: How do you inspect and change Macie configuration?
interview.answer: Use GetMacieSession to read the current status and settings. Use UpdateMacieSession to pause or resume Macie and to change the finding publication frequency.
interview.followUp: Which publication frequencies are valid? FIFTEEN_MINUTES, ONE_HOUR, and SIX_HOURS.

interview.question: What is the difference between pausing and disabling Macie?
interview.answer: Disabling Macie stops all activities and permanently deletes its settings, resources, and stored data, including findings and classification jobs.

The account administration API lets you read status and selected account settings.
Finding updates can be published every 15 minutes, hour, or six hours.
Policy findings report S3 bucket changes that may reduce security or privacy.
Sensitive data findings report detected sensitive data in S3 objects.
After enablement, Macie builds an inventory of S3 general purpose buckets in the Region.
gotchas: Macie is Regional. Enable it separately in every Region where you want to use it.
Disabling is destructive: Macie permanently deletes findings, jobs, custom data identifiers, and the session resource.
A Macie administrator must remove or disassociate member accounts before suspending or disabling Macie.

MemoryDB.explanation: A MemoryDB cluster runs inside an Amazon VPC. You choose its engine, node type, shards, replicas, network access, encryption, snapshots, maintenance settings, and optional notifications. interview.question: What is configured when creating a MemoryDB cluster?
interview.answer: A MemoryDB cluster is created inside an Amazon VPC. Its configuration includes the engine, node type, shards, replicas, access controls, network settings, and optional encryption and snapshots.
interview.followUp: What must be configured before clients connect? Network access must be authorized, including suitable security group rules and MemoryDB access control settings.

interview.question: How can you create a cluster from the command line?
interview.answer: The AWS CLI command uses `create-cluster` with values such as the cluster name, node type, ACL, engine, and subnet group. The documentation shows Valkey as an example engine.
interview.followUp: How would you make the cluster more available? Use multiple shards and replicas, and ensure Multi-AZ has at least one replica per shard.

interview.question: When can an application connect to the cluster?

interview.followUp: What should you do after a temporary test? Delete the cluster so active hourly charges stop.

keyPoints: MemoryDB clusters run in an Amazon VPC.
Use at least two shards when you want higher availability.
Parameter groups define runtime settings for the cluster.
Security groups control which network traffic can reach the cluster.
Encryption at rest protects data stored on disk.
Encryption in transit protects data while it moves across the network.
Automatic snapshots are enabled by default in the console.
gotchas: The cluster is billed while it is active, even when it is not being used. Delete it after testing to stop charges.
Multi-AZ requires at least one replica in every shard.
Billing starts when the cluster is available, including for a partial hour.

MSK.sourceTitle: Welcome to the Amazon MSK Developer Guide
MSK.summary: Amazon MSK is a fully managed service for running Apache Kafka applications that process streaming data. AWS manages cluster operations, while applications use standard Kafka operations to produce and consume data.
MSK.explanation: Amazon MSK manages Apache Kafka cluster operations for you, while your applications use standard Kafka operations to produce and consume data. You can manage clusters through the AWS console, AWS CLI, or SDK APIs. MSK uses open-source Apache Kafka versions, so existing Kafka applications, tools, and plugins can work without application-code changes.

interview.question: What is Amazon MSK?
interview.answer: Amazon MSK is a managed service for running applications that use Apache Kafka for streaming data. AWS handles control-plane tasks such as creating, updating, and deleting clusters, while applications use Kafka data-plane operations.
interview.followUp: What happens when a broker fails? MSK detects common failures and mitigates or replaces the unhealthy broker; applications can continue using the same broker IP addresses after recovery.

interview.question: How can you manage an MSK cluster?
interview.answer: You can manage MSK clusters with the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or SDK APIs. These interfaces support operations such as creating, deleting, listing, viewing, and updating clusters.
interview.followUp: Why should the CLI be upgraded? The documentation says to use the latest version so it supports the MSK features described in the guide.

interview.question: Why can existing Kafka applications work with MSK?
interview.answer: MSK runs open-source Apache Kafka versions. Existing Kafka applications, tools, and partner or community plugins can therefore be used without changing application code.
interview.followUp: What does MSK provide for metadata management? In KRaft mode, Kafka controllers propagate cluster metadata instead of ZooKeeper nodes, and MSK manages these controllers without extra setup.

keyPoints: MSK is a fully managed service for applications that process streaming data with Apache Kafka.
MSK runs open-source Apache Kafka versions, supporting existing Kafka tools and plugins.
An MSK cluster can use a Kafka version listed in the service's supported-version documentation.
Use the AWS console, AWS CLI, or SDK APIs to perform MSK control-plane operations.
MSK automatically detects and recovers from common cluster failures to reduce disruption to producers and consumers.
KRaft controllers manage Kafka metadata without extra MSK cost, setup, or customer management.
gotchas: Use the latest AWS CLI before using documented MSK features. Configure the CLI after installing or upgrading it.
MSK manages control-plane tasks, but applications still use Kafka data-plane operations for topics and message flow.

Neptune.summary: The Amazon Neptune client is a low-level interface for managing Neptune resources. It supports operations for clusters, instances, snapshots, parameter groups, and other database resources.
Neptune.explanation: The Amazon Neptune client is a low-level interface for managing Neptune resources through a programming or command-line interface. Create it with the service name `neptune`, then call operations such as creating clusters, describing resources, or managing snapshots. Some operations are asynchronous, so the result may require polling or a waiter before the change is complete.
Neptune.returns: Client operations return operation-specific response objects. The page does not define one common return type.

example.code:
import boto3

client = boto3.client("neptune", region_name="us-east-1")
response = client.describe_db_clusters()

for cluster in response.get("DBClusters", []):
    print(cluster["DBClusterIdentifier"], cluster["Status"])
example.explanation: This creates a low-level Neptune client and lists database clusters with their identifiers and statuses.

interview.question: How do you create a Neptune service client?
interview.answer: Create a session and call `create_client("neptune")`. The resulting low-level client exposes operations for managing Neptune infrastructure, such as clusters, instances, parameter groups, snapshots, and subscriptions.
interview.followUp: How can a program wait for a database instance to become ready? Use the client waiter for `DBInstanceAvailable` and wait until the operation reaches that state.

interview.question: Which graph models and query languages does Neptune support?
interview.answer: Neptune supports property graphs and W3C RDF graphs. The documented query languages for these models include Gremlin and SPARQL.
interview.followUp: Which model does RDF represent? RDF is the W3C graph model, while a property graph is the other supported model.

interview.question: How should code handle asynchronous Neptune operations?
interview.answer: Neptune API calls can be asynchronous. A caller must determine whether a command has been applied by polling, using a callback, or using an available waiter.
interview.followUp: Which waiters are listed for the client? The page lists `DBInstanceAvailable` and `DBInstanceDeleted`.

keyPoints: The client is a low-level interface for Amazon Neptune.
Neptune supports both property graph and W3C RDF data models.
Gremlin is used with property graphs, and SPARQL is used with RDF graphs.
The client provides management operations, including role changes, tags, clusters, instances, snapshots, and parameter groups.
A client can provide waiters through `get_waiter` for supported resource states.
gotchas: A request may not finish immediately. Use polling, callbacks, or a waiter when the operation is asynchronous.
Check each operation's parameter documentation because changes can apply immediately, after a reboot, or during a maintenance window.

interview.followUp: Can the CLI be skipped? Yes. The console does not require the AWS CLI.

interview.question: What problem does AWS Organizations solve?
interview.answer: AWS Organizations groups AWS accounts and lets you manage them together. It supports account creation, invitations, and policy-based controls across the organization.
interview.followUp: What can an organizational unit contain? An OU can contain accounts and other OUs, which lets you build a hierarchy for applying policies.

interview.question: What is an organizational unit?
interview.answer: An organizational unit is a container in an organization hierarchy. The CLI creates one by receiving a parent ID and a name.
interview.followUp: Why use nested OUs? Nested OUs help organize accounts into multiple levels, such as environment and team, so policies can target the right group.

interview.question: How do you attach a policy?

interview.question: How do you create an Amazon Personalize solution?

interview.question: How does automatic training work?

interview.question: How is an active solution version used?

interview.followUp: How can you monitor training? List solution versions to find the version ARN, then describe the solution version to check its status.

interview.question: What problem does AWS PrivateLink solve?
interview.answer: AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity from a VPC to supported AWS services, endpoint services, and other resources. It uses VPC endpoints, so the connection does not require an internet gateway or public IP address.
interview.followUp: How can a private subnet use an AWS service name? Enable private DNS for an interface endpoint. Requests to the service's normal public DNS name then resolve to private endpoint network-interface addresses.

interview.question: How do VPC endpoints work with PrivateLink?
interview.answer: A VPC endpoint is the access point that lets VPC resources reach a supported service privately. Interface endpoints create endpoint network interfaces in selected subnets, while gateway endpoints use route tables for supported services such as Amazon S3.
interview.followUp: How should interface endpoint availability be designed? Place endpoint network interfaces in at least two Availability Zones and run dependent resources in those zones.

interview.question: What are the main operational and cost considerations?
interview.answer: Interface endpoints are billed by provisioned endpoint-hours in each Availability Zone and by the amount of data processed. The documentation recommends at least two Availability Zones for production resilience.
interview.followUp: What happens if one Availability Zone fails? With endpoint network interfaces in multiple zones, traffic can use a healthy interface; a single-zone endpoint can lose access when that zone is impaired.

keyPoints: PrivateLink makes supported services and resources reachable through private VPC connectivity.
VPC endpoints can provide access across VPC and AWS account boundaries.
A provider can publish its own endpoint service for other AWS customers to use.
An interface endpoint creates a network interface in each selected subnet.
Endpoint network-interface IP addresses stay unchanged while the endpoint exists.
Use at least two Availability Zones to improve endpoint availability and resilience.
gotchas: Interface endpoints have hourly charges in each Availability Zone, plus charges for processed data.
The connection is initiated from resources in the VPC; the service cannot start requests through the endpoint.
To resolve endpoint names from on-premises networks, use Route 53 Resolver endpoints and Resolver rules.

Provisioned Concurrency.sourceTitle: Configuring provisioned concurrency for an Event Function - AWS Lambda
Provisioned Concurrency.summary: Provisioned concurrency prepares Lambda execution environments before requests arrive. It reduces cold-start latency for functions that need fast responses.
Provisioned Concurrency.explanation: Lambda prepares the requested number of execution environments before requests arrive. Initialization code runs while Lambda allocates these environments, so handler calls can avoid cold-start initialization. If traffic exceeds the provisioned amount, Lambda uses on-demand environments for the extra requests.
Provisioned Concurrency.syntax: aws lambda put-provisioned-concurrency-config --function-name FUNCTION_NAME --qualifier ALIAS_OR_VERSION --provisioned-concurrent-executions NUMBER

parameters.name: function-name
parameters.description: The function name or function ARN.

parameters.name: qualifier
parameters.description: A published version or alias. The setting cannot use $LATEST.

parameters.name: provisioned-concurrent-executions
parameters.description: The number of execution environments to prepare.

Provisioned Concurrency.returns: The CLI operation reports the requested and allocated provisioned concurrency, status, and last modification time.

example.title: Set provisioned concurrency
example.code:
aws lambda put-provisioned-concurrency-config \
  --function-name my-function \
  --qualifier BLUE \
  --provisioned-concurrent-executions 100
example.explanation: This gives the BLUE alias of my-function 100 ready execution environments.

useCases.title: Reduce interactive request latency
useCases.scenario: A web or mobile application needs low latency for user requests.

useCases.title: Scale on a schedule
useCases.scenario: Traffic follows a known daily or weekly pattern.

useCases.title: Scale with target tracking
useCases.scenario: Traffic changes unpredictably and the function should keep a target utilization.

interview.question: What is provisioned concurrency?
interview.answer: Provisioned concurrency is the number of execution environments that Lambda initializes before requests arrive. It helps reduce cold-start latency, especially for interactive applications.
interview.followUp: What happens if traffic is higher than the configured amount? Lambda uses on-demand environments for the excess traffic, so those requests can still have cold-start latency.

interview.question: How do you estimate the required amount?
interview.answer: Use the concurrency estimate: average requests per second multiplied by average request duration in seconds. Lambda also suggests adding a 10 percent buffer to the usual peak.
interview.followUp: How would you measure the inputs? Use the Invocation metric for request rate and the Duration metric for average duration.

interview.question: What must be true for invocations to use provisioned concurrency?
interview.answer: Apply the setting to a published version or alias. If an event source invokes a different version or alias, it will not use the prepared environments.
interview.followUp: Can reserved and provisioned concurrency be combined? Yes, but provisioned concurrency cannot be greater than the function's reserved concurrency.

keyPoints: The setting is a number of execution environments prepared before invocation.
Provisioned concurrency adds charges, unlike reserved concurrency.
Estimate concurrency by multiplying average request rate by average request duration.
Add a 10 percent buffer to the normal peak when choosing the value.
Move reusable setup outside the handler so it runs during environment allocation.
The initialization-type environment variable stays unchanged for an environment.
gotchas: Configure provisioned concurrency on a published version or alias, not on $LATEST.
Provisioned concurrency does not cap traffic. Extra requests can use on-demand environments.
Initialization and continuously allocated provisioned concurrency can create charges even when requests do not use an environment.

interview.question: How are the TTL timestamps calculated?
interview.answer: The code gets the current time, converts it to epoch seconds, and adds 90 days to create the expiration timestamp. It stores these values in createdAt and expireAt.

interview.followUp: What input does the function need? It needs a table name, Region, partition-key value, and sort-key value.
